title: Chapter 1: India–Pakistan Relations
syllabus: “India and its neighbourhood — relations.” The chapter covers cross-border terrorism, the Indus Waters Treaty, Siachen and Sir Creek, ceasefire regimes, the Kartarpur Corridor and the geopolitics of Article 370.

sections.title: Background: Key Terms and Evolution of Relations

blocks.html: India and Pakistan share a frontier of about 3,323 km, the Indus basin and four wars (1947–48, 1965, 1971, 1999); both have been declared nuclear-weapon states since 1998. Every normalisation attempt (Shimla 1972, Lahore 1999, the Composite Dialogue of 2004–08) was broken by a terror attack traced to Pakistan-based groups. After the Pahalgam attack (22 April 2025, 26 killed), India held the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) in abeyance and launched Operation Sindoor (7–10 May 2025); India’s position now is that “terror and talks cannot go together”.

blocks.title: India–Pakistan relations: milestones, 1947 to 2025
blocks.caption: Each attempt at peace (Tashkent, Shimla, Lahore, the Composite Dialogue) was followed by a war or a major terror attack. Since 2016 India’s responses to attacks have become military and public.

blocks.label: CASE STUDY
blocks.html: Pahalgam to Operation Sindoor, 2025. 22 April: 25 tourists and a local pony operator killed at Baisaran after victims were asked their religion. 23 April: Cabinet Committee on Security held the IWT in abeyance, closed Attari, cancelled SAARC visas, expelled defence attachés. 24 April: Pakistan closed its airspace, suspended trade, threatened to hold Shimla in abeyance. 7 May: India struck nine terror sites including Bahawalpur (JeM) and Muridke (LeT), calling the action “focused, measured and non-escalatory” (PIB). 7–10 May: Pakistani drones and shelling, especially on Poonch, mostly intercepted (Akash, S-400); India hit 11 air bases including Nur Khan. 10 May: DGMO call; firing stopped at 17:00 IST.

blocks.text: 11.1 Terrorism and the Future of SAARC

blocks.tag: UPSC MAINS 2016 · GS PAPER II · 12.5 MARKS · 200 WORDS
blocks.question: "Increasing cross-border terrorist attacks in India and growing interference in the internal affairs of several member-states by Pakistan are not conducive for the future of SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation)." Explain with suitable examples.

blocks.html: SAARC (1985) works by consensus and needs a minimum of trust among its eight members. Terror attacks traced to Pakistan have broken that trust: the 19th summit at Islamabad (2016) was cancelled after Uri, and no summit has been held since Kathmandu (2014).

items.label: Terror blocks summits
items.html: after Uri (September 2016), India, Bangladesh, Afghanistan, Bhutan and Sri Lanka withdrew from the Islamabad summit, which was then cancelled

items.label: Interference beyond India
items.html: Afghanistan accused Pakistan of sheltering the Taliban; Bangladesh objected to Pakistan’s statements on its 1971 war-crimes trials

items.label: Connectivity blocked
items.html: Pakistan refused to sign the SAARC Motor Vehicles Agreement (2014) and denies transit to Afghanistan, so India moved to BBIN and BIMSTEC

items.label: Trade stalled
items.html: SAFTA has not delivered; intra-regional trade remains about 5% of South Asia’s total trade

blocks.html: Pursue sub-regional and BIMSTEC cooperation; keep SAARC’s technical bodies (the SAARC Development Fund, the South Asian University) alive; tie any summit to action on terror.
Regional integration needs a terror-free environment. Until Pakistan acts, South Asian cooperation will move through BIMSTEC and bilateral corridors rather than SAARC.

blocks.tag: UPSC MAINS 2015 · GS PAPER II · 12.5 MARKS · 200 WORDS
blocks.question: Terrorist activities and mutual distrust have clouded India-Pakistan relations. To what extent the use of soft power like sports and cultural exchanges could help generate goodwill between the two countries? Discuss with suitable examples.

blocks.html: Soft power, in Joseph Nye’s sense, is the ability to attract rather than coerce. India and Pakistan share language, music, cuisine, cricket and sacred sites, but attacks from 26/11 to Pahalgam (2025) have repeatedly overwhelmed this shared capital.

items.label: Cricket diplomacy
items.html: Zia-ul-Haq’s visit to Jaipur (1987) eased the Brasstacks crisis; the 2004 tour built support for the Composite Dialogue

items.label: Religious diplomacy
items.html: the Kartarpur Corridor (2019) gave visa-free access to Sikh pilgrims; the 1974 shrines protocol still runs

items.label: Culture and humanitarian gestures
items.html: films, music, Urdu poetry, medical visas and the release of fishermen soften public opinion

items.label: Limits
items.html: goodwill is the first casualty of terror. After Pahalgam, Kartarpur was closed and bilateral sport stopped; the teams meet only in multilateral events. Soft power cannot change the policy of a military establishment that uses proxies

blocks.html: [SKETCH] Two parallel tracks: people-to-people (cricket, Kartarpur, visas) and security (terror, LoC, IWT), with a “terror” arrow cutting across both.
Keep humanitarian and religious channels insulated from crises; support student and Track II exchanges; tie political normalisation to verifiable action on terror.
Soft power can prepare the ground but cannot replace security guarantees. A terror-free environment is the precondition for goodwill to become peace.

blocks.text: 11.3 Operation Sindoor and India’s New Pakistan Doctrine

blocks.question: “Operation Sindoor marked a shift in India’s Pakistan policy from strategic restraint to deterrence by punishment.” Critically examine.

blocks.html: After the Pahalgam attack (22 April 2025, 26 killed), India struck nine terror sites in Pakistan and PoK on 7 May 2025 and then 11 air bases. The doctrine stated on 12 May promised a response on India’s terms, no acceptance of nuclear blackmail and no distinction between terrorists and their sponsors.

items.label: From restraint to retaliation
items.html: no military response to 26/11 (2008); calibrated strikes in 2016 and 2019; open strikes on Pakistan’s heartland and air bases in 2025

items.label: Non-military levers
items.html: the IWT held in abeyance, a full import ban and IMF abstention

items.label: Escalation control
items.html: terror targets first, military targets only after Pakistani attacks; a DGMO-agreed ceasefire on 10 May

blocks.html: [SKETCH] Escalation ladder: Uri 2016 (rung 3), Pulwama 2019 (rung 4), Pahalgam 2025 (rung 5), with the nuclear threshold at the top.

items.html: Terror groups regenerate; Pakistan’s army gained at home; China supplied weapons and inputs
Escalation time is compressed by drones and missiles; the US claimed a mediating role

blocks.html: Combine deterrence by punishment with deterrence by denial (fencing, counter-drone systems, intelligence); keep the hotline and nuclear CBMs; build a coalition against terror financing at FATF and the UN.
Operation Sindoor redrew India’s red lines, but lasting deterrence needs credibility, crisis stability and diplomacy together, in line with India’s strategic autonomy.

items: Four wars (1947–48, 1965, 1971, 1999); the Shimla Agreement (1972) created the LoC and bilateralism.
Frontier: International Border, LoC (about 740 km), AGPL at Siachen (about 110 km), Sir Creek (96 km).
Pahalgam (22 April 2025, 26 killed): IWT in abeyance, Attari closed, visas and Kartarpur suspended.
Operation Sindoor (7–10 May 2025): 9 terror sites, then 11 air bases; DGMO ceasefire on 10 May 2025.
Doctrine of 12 May 2025: response on India’s terms, no nuclear blackmail, no distinction between terrorists and sponsors.
IWT: Eastern rivers to India, Western to Pakistan; Court of Arbitration (August 2026) rejected abeyance; India rejects the court.
Article 370 changes (5 August 2019) upheld by the Supreme Court (11 December 2023); elections held in 2024.
Trade: exports US$ 2.07 billion (2018-19) down to about US$ 0.12 billion in May–October 2025.
CBMs still working: nuclear installation lists (1 January), prisoner lists, DGMO hotline.
China supplies about 81% of Pakistan’s arms imports; Saudi–Pakistan pact (2025) and Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (2026).
